cue.topic: Describe a place in nature that you enjoyed visiting
bullets: when you went there and who you went with
and explain why you enjoyed visiting it

part2.model: I'd like to talk about a lovely day I spent at Ullswater, a long, narrow lake in the Lake District in the north of England. I went there last August with my cousin Priya and two university friends, and we had been looking forward to it for weeks. We set off at dawn and drove for nearly four hours, passing rolling hills dotted with sheep. When we finally arrived, the water was so still that the mountains were reflected perfectly in it. It took my breath away. I had never seen such a calm, beautiful scene. Once we had spread out our picnic by the shore, we hired a small rowing boat and drifted out to the middle of the lake. Later we hiked up a steep path to a viewpoint, where we could see for miles in every direction. Priya, who is a keen photographer, spent ages trying to capture the light as it broke through the clouds. The reason I enjoyed it so much is that everything felt peaceful and far from the hustle and bustle of my daily life. There was no traffic and no phone signal, so we simply talked and laughed. By the time we headed home, I felt completely recharged. That trip reminded me how much I need to get back to nature, and we have already planned to return next summer.

questions.q: To what extent should individuals, rather than governments, be responsible for protecting the environment?
questions.model: To a certain extent, but I'd say governments carry the greater burden. Individuals can recycle and cut down on waste, yet only legislation can force large factories to curb their emissions. Without strict regulations, businesses tend to put profit first. That said, personal choices add up, and consumer pressure can push companies towards greener practices. So I think real progress needs both levels working together. Honestly, neither side can succeed entirely alone.

questions.q: How far can technology be relied upon to solve environmental problems?
questions.model: Technology can certainly help, but it is no silver bullet. Renewable energy, such as solar and wind power, is already reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, and electric vehicles are becoming mainstream. On the other hand, relying solely on innovation may encourage people to carry on consuming as before. In my view, we need to combine new technology with genuine changes in lifestyle. Otherwise, we risk postponing difficult decisions. That balance is the only realistic path forward.
